lesson.title: Reading the Word: Schools, Faith, and Learning in the Colonies
lesson.summary: Colonial education varied sharply by region, with Puritan Massachusetts pioneering town supported schools to promote religious literacy while the Southern colonies relied mainly on private tutoring for the planter elite.
lesson.body:
Education in the colonies grew out of religious conviction as much as any love of learning for its own sake, especially in New England. The Puritans who settled Massachusetts Bay Colony believed every believer needed to read the Bible directly rather than rely entirely on a minister's interpretation, which made literacy a spiritual necessity rather than a luxury. This conviction translated quickly into law and public policy, since the colony's leaders governed with the explicit goal of building a godly, literate community and used the tools of colonial governance, including binding legislation passed by the General Court, to make that goal a reality.

In 1647 the Massachusetts Bay Colony passed a law often nicknamed the Old Deluder Satan Act, because its text explained that Satan wanted to keep people from understanding scripture through ignorance of the language it was written in. The law required any town of fifty or more households to hire a teacher to instruct children in reading and writing, and any town of one hundred or more households to establish a grammar school capable of preparing boys for college. This made Massachusetts Bay one of the first places in the world to require, by law, that communities fund basic education, and other New England colonies soon followed similar patterns.

New England's commitment to education reached its highest level with the founding of Harvard College in 1636, established primarily to train a steady supply of educated ministers for the colony's churches, since the first generation of university trained clergy who had emigrated from England would not live forever. Harvard's founding just sixteen years after the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth signals how urgently New England's leaders treated the task of reproducing an educated, literate religious culture in the new world.

Education looked very different in the Southern colonies. Settlement there was spread across scattered plantations rather than concentrated in towns, which made the New England model of a shared local schoolhouse impractical. Wealthy planter families instead relied on private tutors, sometimes sent their sons to school in England, or grouped children from a few neighboring plantations together under a hired instructor, while poorer families and enslaved children had little or no access to formal schooling at all. The Middle Colonies fell somewhere in between, with schools often organized by particular religious denominations, Quaker, Presbyterian, Dutch Reformed, and others, reflecting the same religious diversity that helped fuel the Great Awakening.

Across all regions, formal education remained overwhelmingly available to boys, while girls typically received only basic literacy, sometimes through informal dame schools run out of a woman's home, since the goal for most girls' education was practical household competence rather than college preparation. These regional patterns, a public, religiously motivated school system in New England, tutoring for the elite in the South, and denominational schooling in the Middle Colonies, illustrate how colonial governance and religious belief together shaped one of the most basic institutions of colonial life long before any unified American approach to education existed.
